newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls against the mark in thin market..
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls against the mark in thin market..

text.p: The dollar dropped against the mark Monday when traders opted to liquidate dollar holdings before Federal Reserve policy-makers meet to discuss interest rates on Tuesday.
Volume was very light with traders wanting to minimise risk before closing their books for the year.
"You'll have a tough time putting much of a spin on anything seen today," said John Beerling, chief dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
"(The Fed meeting) is going to serve to keep us quiet for a little while ... We're looking for no change -- pretty much a steady monetary policy," he added.
The Federal Open Market Committee meets for the last time this year on Tuesday. The Fed has not changed interest rates since February, when it lowered short-term interest rates.
On Monday, the dollar fell to 1.5453 marks from 1.5545 on Friday.
With so many buyers keeping a low profile on the sidelines, the dollar fell swiftly below 1.55 marks as traders exited positions.

A weekend agreement on a budget "Stability Pact" for European Economic and Monetary Union was not initially seen as good news for the German currency since Germany dropped demands that the European Central Bank, and not politicians, enforce budget discipline after countries join the single currency in 1999.

"People are still digesting the EU stabity pact," said John McCarthy of ING Barings Capital Markets. "In general, people are feeling it's a weakish one, which should be positive for the dollar in the short-run.
"But I think the longs on dollar/mark ... were a bit disappointed that they didn't get follow-through," he added.
The mark rose against the yen on Monday but the dollar closed unchanged from Friday at 113.90 yen, after rising earlier in the day.

Traders said the yen fell against the U.S. unit early amid diminished fears that Japan's appetite for U.S. Treasury securities this year, which helped spur the dollar to 42-month highs in October, was eroding.

Last week, convulsed with doubts over whether Japanese investors would sustain their record levels of U.S. bond purchases, Wall Street questioned the longevity of the dollar's recent advance against the yen.

But after steadying, the dollar got an additional boost from an article in the Wall Street Journal saying Japanese fund managers still have a healthy appetite for U.S. bonds, which offer far higher returns than Japanese investments, and may even increase their buying.

"People are sort of looking for reasons why dollar/yen just won't go down," said Anne Pankowski, vice president of foreign exchange at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce in New York. "You can keep pointing to the fact that there is this seemingly fundamental shift in (Japanese) pension funds offshore."
In other trade, the dollar fell to 1.3198 Swiss francs from 1.3250 Swiss on Friday. It rose to Canadian $1.3669 from C$1.3629. The pound rose to $1.6670 from $1.6565 on Friday.
